title: Macroprudential policy and productivity: friends not foes
gist: An ECB Blog post argues macroprudential regulation supports rather than hinders European productivity growth, because financial crises and real-estate credit booms both destroy productivity by misallocating credit away from innovative firms, and recent evidence shows post-2021 capital buffer tightening had minimal cost to overall credit supply.

themes.theme: Reframing macroprudential policy as a productivity tool, not a drag

insights.claim: The ECB argues that, contrary to the suspicion that regulation is to blame for sluggish European productivity growth, macroprudential policy can actually support productivity by helping prevent financial crises and keeping credit flowing to where it matters most.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Pushes back on deregulation narratives tied to European competitiveness debates; investors should not assume looser bank capital rules are the fix for weak euro area productivity.
insights.quote: macroprudential policy can actually support productivity growth, by helping to prevent crises and keep credit flowing where it matters most
insights.locator: opening paragraph

insights.claim: Macroprudential policy has two goals that both benefit productivity: a primary goal of building financial-system resilience to withstand crises, and a secondary goal of guarding against the overconfidence and excessive risk-taking typical of financial booms.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Gives investors a two-track lens for evaluating macroprudential moves: crisis-resilience buffers versus boom-cooling measures like mortgage limits.
insights.locator: Macroprudential policy has two main goals

insights.claim: All euro area countries currently apply some form of macroprudential capital requirement on banks on top of individual banking-supervision requirements, and almost all also impose limits to curb risky mortgage lending, reflecting the significant expansion of macroprudential tools since the 2008 financial crisis.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Confirms macroprudential capital add-ons and mortgage caps are now structural features of euro area bank regulation, not one-off crisis measures, relevant to bank capital and lending forecasts.
insights.locator: The use of macroprudential policies has expanded significantly

insights.claim: Policymakers, including ECB Supervisory Board members, have stressed that simplifying the bureaucratic burden of financial regulation should not translate into loosening financial regulation itself — simplification does not mean deregulation.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Signals the ECB will resist market or industry pressure to use the 'simplification' agenda as cover for weakening capital or mortgage-lending rules.
insights.locator: However, policymakers have stressed

themes.theme: Financial crises leave lasting productivity scars

insights.claim: Growth in output per worker falls by 0.55 percentage points during a typical banking crisis, according to research by Oulton and Sebastiá-Barriel (2016).
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Quantifies the near-term productivity hit from banking crises, a baseline for stress-testing growth forecasts around future credit events.
insights.locator: Growth in output per worker falls by 0.55 percentage points

insights.claim: When banks cut lending during a crisis, firms invest and innovate less and are more likely to fail; because innovation is a cumulative process building on prior inventions, it can take a long time to regain momentum even after activity recovers, while prolonged high unemployment causes deskilling of workers that further damages long-term productivity.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Explains the transmission mechanism from a credit crunch to years of lost innovation and labor-market scarring, useful for modeling recovery speed after a financial shock.
insights.locator: Financial crises are characterised by a sharp drop

insights.claim: The average banking crisis produces an additional long-term 1.1% drop in output per worker for each year the crisis lasts, based on evidence of productivity scarring in the US economy from credit constraints during the 2008 financial crisis (Redmond and Van Zandweghe, 2016).
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Suggests crisis duration, not just severity, should be a key input when estimating productivity losses from a future banking crisis.
insights.locator: The average banking crisis entails an additional long-term 1.1% drop

insights.claim: For a typical five-year banking crisis, the combined short- and long-run effects add up to an 8% total decline in output per worker relative to a no-crisis counterfactual; for context, euro area output per worker has grown by an average of less than 1% per year since 2000.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: An 8% productivity hit dwarfs roughly a decade of average euro area productivity gains, underscoring the outsized economic stakes of preventing banking crises.
insights.locator: For a typical five-year banking crisis

insights.claim: Countercyclical capital buffers (CCyB) require banks to build up capital in good times so they are more resilient when a crisis hits; well-capitalised banks significantly reduce the severity of crisis-driven disruptions to credit supply (Jordà, Richter, Schularick and Taylor, 2021), and macroprudential buffer releases during the Covid-19 pandemic supported euro area banks' capacity to keep supplying credit to firms (Couaillier et al., 2022).
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Real-world evidence (Covid-19 buffer releases) that CCyB design works as intended, supporting continued reliance on releasable capital buffers as a crisis tool.
insights.locator: A key policy tool here are macroprudential capital buffers

insights.claim: The effect of credit supply on total factor productivity (TFP) growth is asymmetric: contractions in credit supply harm TFP growth by halting productivity-enhancing activities, while positive credit supply shocks have only limited effects on productivity (Manaresi and Pierri, 2024).
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Implies macroprudential policy's main productivity value lies in preventing downside credit contractions rather than in stimulating extra credit growth on the upside.
insights.locator: The effect of credit supply is asymmetric

insights.claim: The post-2021 tightening of macroprudential capital buffers in the euro area had a minimal impact on overall bank credit supply, with only a small number of the most capital-constrained banks cutting back lending, and the composition of bank lending (by risk or sector) remained largely unchanged for both constrained and unconstrained banks (Behn, Forletta and Reghezza, 2024).
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Empirical rebuttal to the idea that higher capital buffers meaningfully choke credit to the real economy — argues resilience was bought at low near-term economic cost, weakening the case for loosening buffers to boost lending.
insights.locator: The post-2021 tightening of macroprudential capital buffers

themes.theme: Real estate credit booms crowd out productive, innovative firms

insights.claim: During financial booms, credit tends to flow disproportionately to firms with appreciating tangible assets (especially real estate) rather than to more innovative firms that would use it more productively, diverting resources away from productivity-enhancing activity.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: A structural reason to watch real-estate credit growth as a leading indicator of future misallocation and productivity drag, not just of financial-stability risk.
insights.locator: during financial booms credit tends to flow to firms with appreciating tangible assets

insights.claim: In the run-up to the 2008 crisis in the United States, a one standard deviation increase in house prices in a given region reduced local banks' corporate lending by 42.3% and corporate investment by 20.9% (Chakraborty, Goldstein and MacKinlay, 2018).
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Quantifies how sharply regional house-price surges can crowd out business credit, a benchmark for assessing current euro area housing-market hotspots.
insights.locator: a one standard deviation increase in house prices

insights.claim: During the average credit boom, 70% of new credit goes to households and the less productive non-tradeable sector rather than to more productive tradeable industries, which drives falling aggregate productivity (Müller and Verner, 2024).
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: A rule-of-thumb ratio investors can use to gauge how much of a credit expansion is likely productivity-enhancing versus productivity-eroding.
insights.quote: During the average credit boom 70% of new credit goes to households and the less productive non-tradeable sector.
insights.locator: During the average credit boom

insights.claim: Misallocation of credit among Spanish manufacturing firms — toward those owning appreciating real estate rather than toward more productive firms — accounted for 40% of the decline in Spanish productivity between 2003 and 2007 (Basco, Lopez-Rodriguez and Moral-Benito, 2025).
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: A concrete euro area case study showing collateral-driven credit misallocation can explain a large share of a national productivity slowdown, relevant to assessing Southern European growth trajectories.
insights.locator: the misallocation of credit among Spanish manufacturing firms

insights.claim: Rising real estate prices create a particularly strong disincentive for banks to lend to innovative, R&D-intensive firms, because intangible assets such as intellectual property are less attractive collateral than the appreciating real estate typically owned by less productive firms (Cecchetti and Kharroubi, 2019).
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Highlights a collateral-based structural bias in bank lending against IP-heavy, innovative firms — a factor relevant to why Europe's innovative sectors lean more on equity/VC than bank credit.
insights.locator: Rising real estate prices create a particularly strong disincentive

insights.claim: Recent work by Nobel Prize winner Joseph Stiglitz (with Hirano, 2025) argues that financial regulation limiting the relaxation of lending standards on real-estate-collateralised loans during a financial upswing is required to mitigate the misallocation dynamic that channels credit into real estate at the expense of productive firms.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Cites high-profile academic backing for tightening mortgage-lending standards during booms, strengthening the policy case for borrower-based macroprudential measures.
insights.locator: Recent work by Nobel Prize winner Joseph Stiglitz

insights.claim: Borrower-based measures (BBMs) — limits on bank mortgage lending such as loan-to-income multiples or loan-to-value caps — directly restrain banks' capacity to shift toward risky real estate lending, can in some cases limit the excessive house-price growth driving the misallocation, and make both borrowers and lenders more resilient to downturns, thereby also reducing the likelihood of severe financial crises.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: BBMs are framed as a dual-purpose tool — curbing house-price booms and misallocation while also building crisis resilience — worth tracking as a policy lever across euro area housing markets.
insights.locator: BBMs are limits placed on banks' mortgage lending

themes.theme: Limits of macroprudential policy and complementary levers for productivity

insights.claim: The ECB cautions that ever-tightening macroprudential policy will not result in ever-growing productivity, and that macroprudential policy should continue to be set on the basis of financial stability concerns rather than as a productivity-maximizing tool in itself.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: A guardrail against over-interpreting the productivity argument as a case for unlimited tightening; macroprudential settings will still be calibrated primarily to financial-stability risk.
insights.quote: ever-tightening macroprudential policy will not result in ever-growing productivity
insights.locator: Macroprudential policy helps foster a stable environment

insights.claim: ECB research has highlighted the importance of non-bank financing — such as financial markets and equity investors — for funding risky innovative projects that drive productivity growth, since financing innovative firms often relies more heavily on equity and venture capital than on traditional bank lending (Andreeva et al., 2024).
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Argues that bank-focused macroprudential policy alone cannot fix European innovation funding gaps — equity and VC market depth is the complementary channel to watch.
insights.locator: ECB research has highlighted the importance of non-bank financing

insights.claim: Achieving a more diversified external funding structure in Europe, including through further progress on the capital markets union, could help boost the productivity of euro area firms while also benefiting financial stability.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Positions capital markets union progress as a productivity catalyst investors should track alongside banking regulation, particularly for equity- and VC-dependent innovative firms.
insights.locator: Achieving a more diversified external funding structure

insights.claim: Previous ECB research found that euro area banks hold disproportionate real estate exposures relative to that sector's limited contribution to economic growth (Andreeva et al., 2024), reinforcing the case for borrower-based measures and for diversifying firms' funding sources away from real-estate-collateralised bank credit.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Flags a structural overweight to real estate on euro area bank balance sheets relative to its economic contribution — relevant to bank sector allocation and concentration-risk analysis.
insights.locator: previous ECB research has specifically highlighted euro area banks' disproportionate real estate exposures
